description: DEF CON 33 Voting Village features research, symposium panels, and hands-on evaluations of election technology and physical voting systems. Sessions cover physical security of voting terminals, statistical Risk-Limiting Audits, ballot marking devices, legal safe harbors under the DMCA, and lessons from landmark state security reviews.

talks.title: Fortress Island: Physical Security in Voting Systems
talks.teaser: Reviews publicly documented physical security controls and tamper-evident seals on deployed voting systems, exposing critical weaknesses in hardware defenses.
talks.summary:
Physical Security as a Core Voting System Defense

Voting system architectures rely heavily on keyed physical locks, tamper-evident seals, and serialized security tape to scope voter interaction in semi-private voting booths to intended, safe operations.

Flaws in Hardware Access Controls and Port Isolation

Drew Springall analyzes vendor specifications, jurisdictional manuals, and field deployment reports, demonstrating how standard keyed locks and insecure access panels leave critical I/O ports, administrative interfaces, and memory storage slots accessible to voters.

Limitations of Tamper-Evident Seals

Relying on procedural seal verification as a sole mitigation for known electronic vulnerabilities is fundamentally flawed due to inconsistent inspection training and non-destructive seal bypass techniques.

Recommendations for Resilient Voting Hardware

Securing voting equipment requires eliminating shared mechanical keyways, implementing hardware-enforced port disablement, and pairing physical inspections with cryptographic vote verification.

talks.title: It's Not Safe Yet: Online Voting in Practice
talks.teaser: Examines the systemic security, cryptographic, and client-side malware risks of internet voting in commercial and public election deployments.
talks.summary:
Election Security and Voting Systems

This talk addresses security challenges in voting systems and election infrastructure. The presentation discusses vulnerabilities in voting machines, ballot systems, and implications for maintaining electoral integrity.

(AI summary — Claude Haiku)

talks.title: Is E2E Verifiability a Magic Bullet for Online Voting
talks.teaser: Explains why End-to-End Verifiability (E2E-V) fails to protect online voting systems against client-side endpoint malware and server infrastructure tampering.
talks.summary:
The Promise and Rhetoric of E2E Verifiability

End-to-End Verifiability (E2E-V) is a cryptographic paradigm allowing voters to verify that their votes were cast as intended, recorded as cast, and tallied as recorded, often promoted as a magic bullet for internet voting.

Client-Side Vulnerabilities Outside the Cryptographic Loop

John Odum demonstrates how E2E-V fails to mitigate client-side malware on voter endpoints. Malicious software running on a voter's device can alter ballot selections or deceive voters before cryptographic proofs are generated.

Server-Side and Infrastructure Attack Surfaces

Beyond endpoint risks, centralized election servers and backend tallying infrastructure outside the cryptographic loop remain susceptible to denial of service, configuration sabotage, and server-side compromise.

Disputing Commercial Internet Voting Claims

Evaluating the technical reality of E2E-V against commercial marketing claims highlights that cryptographic verification alone cannot compensate for fundamentally insecure digital voting platforms.

talks.title: CARVER Vuln Analysis & US Voting System
talks.teaser: Applies the military CARVER targeting and vulnerability analysis matrix to evaluate systemic risks and physical attack vectors across the US election system.
talks.summary:
Origins of the CARVER Vulnerability Framework

Developed by the Office of Strategic Services (OSS) during World War II, the CARVER matrix assesses complex systems across six factors: Criticality, Accessibility, Recuperability, Vulnerability, Effect, and Recognizability.

Applying CARVER to Election Infrastructure

The panel evaluates US election infrastructure through the CARVER methodology, modeling the entire voting lifecycle from voter registration databases and ballot printing to physical voting machines and post-election tabulation.

Identifying Systemic Weaknesses and Chokepoints

Applying objective scoring matrices highlights critical infrastructure vulnerabilities, particularly around physical ballot custody chains, supply chain logistics, and centralized county tabulation systems.

Strategic Defense and Threat Mitigation

Using structured threat frameworks like CARVER allows election officials and cybersecurity defenders to prioritize defensive investments, harden physical access controls, and build operational resilience.

talks.title: Risk Limiting Audits: What They Are and Aren't
talks.teaser: Election auditing pioneer Philip Stark details how Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs) provide statistical verification of paper ballots while warning against auditing untrustworthy vote records.
talks.summary:
Principles of Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs)

Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs) provide a rigorous mathematical framework ensuring a large, pre-specified chance of correcting certified election outcomes if tabulation errors or cyber intrusions altered the winner.

Auditing Methods Across Election Types

Philip Stark explains modern RLA statistical sampling methodologies applicable to diverse election contests, including plurality races, supermajority requirements, and multiwinner instant-runoff voting.

The Prerequisite of Trustworthy Paper Ballots

RLAs can verify well-run elections that maintain a rigorous, uncompromised chain of physical paper ballots. However, conducting an RLA on untrustworthy, unverified, or poorly guarded paper records is mere 'security theater.'

Distinguishing Real Audits from Security Theater

Effective election verification requires pairing statistical post-election audits with rigorous physical paper custody and software-independent voter verification.

talks.title: Dominion ICX Simple Hacks Daunting Recoveries
talks.teaser: Demonstrates real-time ballot manipulation on the Dominion ImageCast X touchscreen terminal and explains why recovering from election definition tampering is daunting.
talks.summary:
The Dominion ImageCast X Ballot Marking Device

Ballot Marking Devices (BMDs) like the Dominion ImageCast X present digital touchscreens for voters to make selections and generate printed paper ballots for optical tabulation.

Manipulating Ballot Layouts via Election Definitions

Using a physical Dominion ICX terminal, researchers demonstrate how simple modifications to election definition files (without requiring binary malware injection) can alter candidate ordering, silently remove choices, or present misleading voting instructions.

Daunting Post-Election Detection and Recovery

Because ballot display manipulations directly deceive the voter during selection, detecting and recovering from election definition tampering after polls close is extraordinarily difficult or impossible without full hand recounts of paper records.

Root Cause Analysis and System Design

Analyzing the underlying architectural decisions in BMD firmware reveals how relying on unauthenticated configuration definitions and barcode-encoded ballots creates severe systemic vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Regulatory Failures with Ballot Marking Devices
talks.teaser: Examines regulatory and certification failures surrounding Ballot Marking Devices, focusing on barcode vote encoding and ballot image discrepancies.
talks.summary:
The Fundamental Dilemma of Ballot Marking Devices

Ballot Marking Devices (BMDs) encode voter choices into machine-readable barcodes or QR codes that human voters cannot visually verify before inserting ballots into precinct scanners.

Discrepancies Across Multiple Ballot Records

Marnie Mahoney highlights how BMDs generate three distinct representations of voter intent: encoded barcode images, human-readable text summaries, and digital scanned ballot images, each vulnerable to differing points of failure or manipulation.

Regulatory and Certification Gaps

Federal and state voting system testing standards have lagged behind technological realities, certifying complex computerized ballot markers that fail to guarantee meaningful voter verification.

Advocating for Independent Paper Verification

Reforming election equipment standards requires mandating human-readable, voter-marked hand paper ballots and prohibiting unreadable barcode vote tabulation.

talks.title: When the Paper Trail Leads Nowhere
talks.teaser: Chronicles the technical failures, security vulnerabilities, and recount challenges of Los Angeles County's $300M bespoke VSAP voting system.
talks.summary:
The Rollout of LA County's VSAP System

In the March 2020 California primary, Los Angeles County deployed its $300 million bespoke Voting Solutions for All People (VSAP) system developed by Smartmatic, experiencing severe technical failures and long lines.

Security Vulnerabilities and Closed-Source Compromises

Despite initial public commitments to open-source the voting codebase, the proprietary implementation contained numerous security vulnerabilities and operational flaws that undermined public transparency.

A Local Odyssey: The Long Beach Recount

Ian Patton recounts the firsthand experience of a grassroots government accountability organization requesting a formal hand recount of a razor-thin local ballot measure, exposing significant obstacles in auditing VSAP paper records.

Lessons for Publicly Funded Voting Technology

Evaluating the VSAP rollout demonstrates the critical importance of open-source transparency, independent security testing, and enforceable voter verification standards in public election infrastructure.

talks.title: Protecting Election Researchers Globally
talks.teaser: Advocates for expanding legal safe harbor protections for election security researchers globally, drawing on lessons from research barriers in Nigeria.
talks.summary:
Legal Risks for Global Election Security Researchers

While election security researchers in the United States operate under established vulnerability disclosure frameworks and DMCA exemptions, researchers in the Global South face severe criminalization and political retaliation.

Case Study: Biometric Election Systems in Nigeria

Miracle Owolabi examines legal restrictions and cybercrime statutes in Nigeria that prevented independent researchers from auditing vulnerable biometric voter authentication systems.

Expanding Safe Harbor Protections Internationally

Drawing parallels to landmark US initiatives like California's Top-to-Bottom Review (TTBR), Owolabi argues that international legal safe harbors must protect good-faith election research to safeguard emerging democracies.

Building an Inclusive Global Election Defense Community

Fostering international collaboration between election security researchers strengthens democratic institutions and addresses vulnerabilities in commercially exported voting technologies.

talks.title: A Review of Post Election Audits in Swing States
talks.teaser: Evaluates the effectiveness, rigor, and reliability of post-election audits conducted across seven closely contested swing states following the 2024 election.
talks.summary:
The Essential Criteria for Effective Post-Election Audits

Post-election audits serve as a critical public check on election outcomes, requiring transparent, trustworthy, and statistically meaningful evidence to verify that machine counts accurately reflect voter intent.

Evaluating Swing State Audits After the 2024 Election

Susan Greenhalgh presents an exhaustive review of post-election auditing procedures conducted across seven battleground swing states, analyzing whether statutory audit rules meet rigorous evidentiary standards.

Gaps in Current State Auditing Practices

Many state-mandated audits suffer from limited sample sizes, reliance on machine re-scans rather than hand counts, and lack of public observation, diminishing their ability to detect subtle tabulation anomalies.

Policy Recommendations for Trustworthy Audits

Strengthening post-election confidence requires states to mandate robust Risk-Limiting Audits of paper ballots, ensure transparent public access, and establish clear recount triggers.

talks.title: Evidence Based Elections and Software Independence
talks.teaser: Turing Award winner Ron Rivest explains software independence and evidence-based elections as foundational principles for securing democratic processes.
talks.summary:
The Concept of Software Independence

Coined by cryptographer Ron Rivest, 'Software Independence' states that an undetected change or bug in election software should not be able to cause an undetectable change in the declared election outcome.

Foundations of Evidence-Based Elections

Evidence-based elections require election systems to produce a trustworthy physical audit trail (primarily hand-marked paper ballots) that can independently prove the accuracy of certified election results.

Limitations of Purely Electronic Voting Systems

Direct Recording Electronic (DRE) systems and paperless internet voting cannot achieve software independence because voters cannot verify that software accurately recorded their intent.

Practical Implementation in Modern Elections

Implementing evidence-based election frameworks combines voter-verified paper ballots with statistical Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs), providing verifiable mathematical resilience against cyber threats.

talks.title: DMCA Security Research Exemption and Election Security
talks.teaser: Breaks down the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) Section 1201 security research exemptions that protect independent voting system audits at the Voting Village.
talks.summary:
The DMCA Section 1201 Landscape

Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) criminalizes circumventing technological protection measures controlling access to copyrighted software, historically chilling independent security research.

The Voting System Research Exemption

Tori Noble details the specific triennial DMCA exemption granted by the US Copyright Office for good-faith security research on voting machines, election hardware, and voter registration systems.

Enabling Community Audits at the Voting Village

This crucial legal safe harbor allows cybersecurity researchers at the DEF CON Voting Village and academic institutions to physically audit voting hardware and disclose vulnerabilities without fear of civil or criminal copyright liability.

Future Policy Reforms for Permanent Safe Harbors

While triennial exemptions provide temporary relief, advocates continue to push for permanent statutory reforms protecting public interest security research.

talks.title: A NY Legal Challenge to ExpressVote XL's Barcode Use
talks.teaser: Susan Lerner reviews the legal challenge in Common Cause NY v. Kosinski against the ES&S ExpressVote XL over barcode vote encoding and voter verifiability laws.
talks.summary:
The ExpressVote XL All-in-One Voting Terminal

The ES&S ExpressVote XL combines ballot marking and optical tabulation into a single touchscreen device, recording voter choices in 1D barcodes and 2D QR codes.

Legal Arguments in Common Cause NY v. Kosinski

Susan Lerner details the New York state court challenge arguing that tabulating votes from unreadable barcodes violates New York statutory requirements and the federal Help America Vote Act (HAVA) guaranteeing voter-verifiable ballots.

The Controversy of Barcode-Based Tabulation

State-level bans on barcode voting in Colorado and federal executive proposals reflect growing bipartisan consensus that voters must be able to visually verify the exact medium used for tabulation.

Potential Nationwide Impact on Voting Machine Regulation

A ruling against barcode-encoded ballots in New York sets significant legal precedents for voting equipment procurement and verification across other US jurisdictions.

talks.title: When Insiders Are the Threat
talks.teaser: Examines multi-state insider access schemes where voting machine software and system images were illicitly copied across Colorado, Georgia, Michigan, and Pennsylvania.
talks.summary:
The Rise of Insider Threats in Election Administration

While election security traditionally focused on external nation-state cyberattacks, recent years have seen coordinated insider access breaches orchestrated by local officials and external partisans.

Multi-State Voting Software Breaches (2020-2022)

The panel details documented breaches across Colorado, Georgia, Michigan, and Pennsylvania where unauthorized actors obtained full forensic disk images and proprietary source code of commercial voting systems.

Implications of Purloined Election Software

Distributing voting system software, firmware keys, and election definitions into the wild lowers the barrier for adversaries to discover zero-day exploits and construct targeted malicious payloads for future elections.

Hardening Physical and Operational Access Controls

Addressing insider threats requires strict multi-custody access controls, enhanced forensic logging of machine maintenance, and proactive software hash verification before election certification.

talks.title: Reflections on TTBR & Everest
talks.teaser: Core researchers and public officials reflect on California's landmark Top-to-Bottom Review (TTBR) and Ohio's EVEREST study, evaluating their legacy for election security.
talks.summary:
The Origins of State-Sponsored Voting Security Reviews

In the mid-2000s, California Secretary of State Debra Bowen and Ohio Secretary of State Jennifer Brunner commissioned independent academic computer scientists to conduct unprecedented security reviews of all certified voting systems.

Methodologies of the TTBR and EVEREST Studies

Researchers including Matt Blaze reflect on the intensive red-team audits and source code reviews that exposed pervasive architectural flaws, default cryptographic keys, and exploitable hardware ports across major voting vendors.

Catalyzing National Election Security Reforms

The findings spurred a nationwide shift away from paperless Direct Recording Electronic (DRE) voting machines toward voter-verified paper ballots and established standards for independent security auditing.

Applying Historic Lessons to Current Election Threats

Evaluating the legacy of the TTBR and EVEREST studies highlights that open, adversarial security evaluation remains vital as election infrastructure incorporates modern connected technologies.

talks.title: History and Significance of the TTBR and PEASWG
talks.teaser: Former California Secretary of State Debra Bowen presents the history and enduring significance of the Top-to-Bottom Review (TTBR) and post-election audit working groups.
talks.summary:
The Crisis of Faith in Electronic Voting in the 2000s

Following widespread adoption of uncertified electronic voting machines after the Help America Vote Act, alarming reports of lost votes and vendor irregularities threatened public trust in American elections.

Launching the California Top-to-Bottom Review (TTBR)

Upon taking office, California Secretary of State Debra Bowen initiated the landmark 2007 Top-to-Bottom Review, enlisting top academic researchers and legal experts to comprehensively audit all voting systems certified in California.

Courageous Policy Decertification and National Impact

Based on findings of severe vulnerabilities, Bowen conditionally decertified vulnerable machines, mandating paper audit trails and setting new standards for post-election audit security working groups (PEASWG).

Enduring Lessons for Democratic Governance

Bowen reflects on the political courage required to prioritize cybersecurity and transparency over vendor resistance, emphasizing that verifiable paper ballots remain the cornerstone of secure elections.

talks.title: Welcome and Introductions
talks.teaser: Organizers welcome attendees to the DEF CON 33 Voting Village, introducing the symposium schedule, hands-on hacking labs, and voting machine targets.
talks.summary:
Welcome to the DEF CON 33 Voting Village

The Voting Village brings together election officials, cybersecurity researchers, voting rights advocates, and hackers to evaluate and strengthen election technology.

Symposium Sessions and Keynote Highlights

Organizers preview the comprehensive talk tracks covering physical voting machine security, post-election statistical audits, legal safe harbors, and international election research.

Hands-On Voting Machine Hacking Labs

Attendees are invited into the interactive Voting Village lab to perform hands-on security evaluations of commercial ballot marking devices, optical scanners, and electronic pollbooks.

Advancing Transparency in Election Security

Emphasizing ethical vulnerability research, the organizers encourage constructive dialogue between the hacker community and election administrators to bolster democratic resilience.
